newsitem.title: INDONESIA: OPINION-LQ45 membership may have few privileges.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-LQ45 membership may have few privileges.

text.p: By David Oxtoby, President Director
PT Asia Equity Jasereh, Jakarta
JAKARTA, Feb 20 - Starting next Monday, February 24, there will be a new index to watch in Jakarta.

This index is intended to represent the 45 largest and most liquid of the JSE's 258 stocks. The index has been created based on trading from mid-July 1994 through the end of 1996, and will be updated quarterly in the future.

With a number of market barometers already available and widely used by investors -- including the MSCI, FT and JF indices -- it is doubtful that inclusion in the LQ45 is going to be a particular boon for constituent stocks.

In the short term, the quarterly revisions may provide occasion for local punters to have some fun with specific counters, but we do not think that membership will initially have the same rewards that inclusion in the 39-stock MSCI is widely believed to have (e.g. greater likelihood to be bought by international institutional investors).
Over several years, however, the LQ45 may emerge as the benchmark index for Indonesia.
ADVANTAGES?

Of course one might be tempted to imagine that PT Tempo Scan Pacific, the smallest stock to be included in the LQ45, now has some advantage in terms of profile or research coverage over rival pharmaceutical maker PT Darya Varia Laboratories, which didn't make the cut.

Any satisfaction is likely to be short-lived, however, as the presence of several large companies such as Jasa Marga, Aneka Tambang and two PLN subsidiaries in Indonesia's IPO pipeline virtually ensures that the smaller LQ45 companies such as Tempo Scan will be unceremoniously bumped off the list in future revisions.

One clear beneficiary from the launch of the LQ45 is the Indonesian government, which will be able to use its clout to have big state privatisations included in the index at the first possible revision, rather than having the matter out of its control, as is the case with the MSCI Indonesia index, which has yet to include BNI 46.
BETTER PERFORMANCE?
Do size and blue-chip status imply better share price performance?

In the early 1990s, when foreign investors accounted for more than 80 percent of the total value of shares traded on the JST, it could be shown empirically that the large, liquid shares sought by foreigners outperformed in rising markets and underperformed in falling ones.
When the JSE hit a five-year peak of 612.9 in January 1994 the premiums for foreign shares versus their local counterparts were also at record highs.
More recently, however, local participation has increased greatly (accurate figures are not available) and smaller cap stocks have been some of the star performers.

If we calculate the LQ45 performance retrospectively for 1996, for example, we can see that it underperformed the market, rising only 20.6 percent versus the JSE's 24.1 percent gain for the year -- implying much better average performance for the more than 200 JSE stocks not included in the LQ45.
BIG CAPS CATCH UP?
That said, we do not think that the big cap stocks will play catch up in the near future.

With the JSE now priced at more than 15x forecast 1997 earnings, we believe investors are hunting for value and will be attracted to companies on less demanding multiples, especially those counters which historically may not have been that liquid but have become more so with the market's improved daily volumes.

Among our favourites: pharmaceutical maker Tempo Scan Pacific (potential exclusion from LQ45 notwithstanding), distributor PT Wicaksana Overseas International, fixed-income specialist Bank Bira and transport operator PT Steady Safe.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
